summary.text: Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire and came from Persis; he lived from about 600 to 530 BC.
He defeated the Median Empire, then conquered Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, building what soon became the largest empire in history at the time.
He was known for tolerating the customs and religions of conquered peoples, and Judaism exalts him for freeing the Jews from the Babylonian captivity.

facts.label: Tomb
facts.value: Pasargadae, revered by millions in modern Iran

items.prompt: A conquered people asks to keep its own customs and gods. What was Cyrus's habitual policy toward such peoples?

options.label: Forced adoption of Persian gods
Tolerance for their customs and religions
Moving them to his capital
Taxing them more heavily for it

items.explain: To the Greeks he was renowned for his habitual policy of tolerance for peoples' customs and religions in the lands he conquered.

items.prompt: Jews held in Babylonian captivity came under Persian rule after Cyrus took Babylon. What did his Edict of Restoration allow?

options.label: Staying in Babylon under Persian protection
Settling in Persis near his capital
Joining his army against the Massagetae
Returning to Judah and rebuilding Jerusalem's Temple

items.explain: He freed the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity, and his efforts enabled their return and the completion of the Second Temple.

items.prompt: A realm this huge needs a way to govern distant lands. What system did Cyrus help develop?

options.label: A central administration at his capital to govern the satraps
Direct rule of every province by the king in person
Self-governing cities that sent only soldiers
Rule by Median generals alone

items.explain: He was influential in developing a central administration at his capital to govern the Achaemenid Empire's satraps.

items.prompt: Accounts differ on how Cyrus died. What does Xenophon say?

options.label: He fell fighting the Massagetae by the Syr Darya
He died at Babylon after the city fell
He did not die fighting but returned to Pasargadae
He was killed by his son Cambyses II

items.explain: One account has him dying in battle with the Massagetae, but Xenophon says he did not die fighting and returned to the capital, Pasargadae.

items.prompt: Later Persian empires looked back at Cyrus's era. How did they view it?

options.label: As a failure to avoid repeating
As a myth with no real history
As a time of foreign rule they resented
With deference, as the ideal example to emulate

items.explain: Future Persian empires often viewed the Achaemenid era with deference and as the ideal example to emulate.

items.prompt: After conquering Lydia and then the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which regions did Cyrus control as a result?

options.label: Egypt and Nubia
Anatolia and the Fertile Crescent
Greece and Scythia
Cyrenaica and the Balkans

items.explain: Conquering Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire gave him control of Anatolia and the Fertile Crescent respectively; Egypt and Nubia fell later under Cambyses II.

paragraphs.heading: Founder of an empire
paragraphs.text: Cyrus II of Persia, usually called Cyrus the Great, lived from about 600 to 530 BC and founded the Achaemenid Empire. Coming from Persis, he defeated the Median Empire and so lifted his family line, the Achaemenid dynasty, to power. He then conquered Lydia, which gave him Anatolia, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which gave him the Fertile Crescent. His realm spread over most of West Asia and much of Central Asia, and it soon became the largest empire the world had yet seen.

paragraphs.heading: His family line
paragraphs.text: The dynasty was named after Achaemenes, who built the state of Parsumash in southwest Iran. His successor Teispes seized the city of Anshan and took the title King of Anshan, which then passed to Teispes' son Cyrus I and on to Cambyses I. Cyrus the Great was the son of Cambyses I, who had named him after his own father. In the Cyrus Cylinder, Cyrus describes himself as the son of Cambyses, great king, king of Anshan.

paragraphs.heading: A tolerant conqueror
paragraphs.text: The Greeks knew him as Cyrus the Elder, and scholars are especially struck by his habit of tolerating the customs and religions of the peoples he conquered. Judaism honours him for ending the Babylonian captivity: after the Persians took Babylon, he issued the Edict of Restoration, and displaced Jews went back to what had been the Kingdom of Judah. He also supported their hopes for a new Temple in Jerusalem, where Solomon's Temple had once stood. That effort ended in the completed Second Temple, which opened the Second Temple period.

paragraphs.heading: Remembered in Isaiah and Iran
paragraphs.text: The Book of Isaiah says Yahweh anointed him and names him messiah for this task; he is the only non-Jew honoured in this way. In Iran his reign helped shape the country's history for well over a thousand years, because later Persian empires looked back on the Achaemenid age as the ideal to copy. He is still revered in modern Iran, where millions treat his tomb at Pasargadae as a place of honour.

paragraphs.heading: Ruler and strategist
paragraphs.text: Cyrus is also remembered for what he achieved in politics and military strategy. He helped build a system of central government, run from his capital, to oversee the empire's satraps, who worked for the benefit of rulers and subjects alike. Over time the prestige of his realm reached as far west as Athens. There, upper-class Greeks took up parts of the culture of the Persian ruling class as their own.

paragraphs.heading: How he died
paragraphs.text: Cyrus led a major campaign into Central Asia. By one account he died in December 530 BC along the Syr Darya, in battle against the Massagetae, a nomadic Eastern Iranian people. Xenophon of Athens told it differently: in his version Cyrus did not fall in battle but went back to his capital, Pasargadae. His son Cambyses II followed him and, in a short reign, conquered Egypt, Nubia and Cyrenaica.

paragraphs.heading: What his name meant
paragraphs.text: The name Cyrus is a Latin form of the Greek Kỹros, which comes from the Old Persian Kūruš. Its meaning is debated. The Greek historians Ctesias and Plutarch said he was named from the Sun, which some read as like the Sun; another proposal is humiliator of the enemy in verbal contest. Some scholars think the name is not Iranian at all but Elamite, meaning he who bestows care.
